questions.stem: What is the empirical formula of butane, C₄H₁₀?
questions.explanation: An empirical formula is the simplest whole-number ratio of atoms. C₄H₁₀ divides by 2 to give C₂H₅, which cannot be simplified further. C₄H₁₀ is the molecular formula, not the empirical one.

questions.stem: In a skeletal formula of a hydrocarbon, what does each end of a line and each corner represent?
options: A covalent bond between a carbon atom and a hydrogen atom
A carbon atom with enough hydrogen atoms to make four bonds
A hydrogen atom bonded to the carbon chain at that point
A carbon atom with no hydrogen atoms attached to it
questions.explanation: Skeletal formulae show only the carbon framework. Every end and corner is a carbon atom, and the hydrogen atoms needed to give each carbon four bonds are understood rather than drawn.

questions.stem: A skeletal formula is a zigzag of five line segments, with a double line between the second and third carbon atoms. What is the molecular formula of the compound?
questions.explanation: Five segments join six carbon atoms. With one C=C double bond the compound is an alkene, CₙH₂ₙ, so it is C₆H₁₂ (hex-2-ene). C₅H₁₀ comes from counting segments instead of carbon atoms.

questions.stem: A hydrocarbon contains 85.7% carbon by mass and has a molar mass of 56.1 g mol⁻¹. Use C = 12.01, H = 1.008. What is its molecular formula?
questions.explanation: Moles in 100 g: C 85.7/12.01 = 7.14 and H 14.3/1.008 = 14.2, a 1 : 2 ratio, so the empirical formula is CH₂ (14.03 g mol⁻¹). 56.1/14.03 = 4, so the molecular formula is C₄H₈. CH₂ is only the empirical formula.

questions.stem: Butane and 2-methylpropane are structural isomers. What does this mean?
options: Compounds with the same molecular formula but different structural formulae
Compounds with the same structural formula but different molecular formulae
Atoms of one element with the same atomic number but different mass numbers
Compounds in the same homologous series that differ by one CH₂ group
questions.explanation: Structural isomers share a molecular formula, such as C₄H₁₀, but their atoms are joined in a different order. Atoms differing only in mass number are isotopes, not isomers.

questions.stem: How many structural isomers are there of hexane, C₆H₁₄?
questions.explanation: They are hexane, 2-methylpentane, 3-methylpentane, 2,2-dimethylbutane and 2,3-dimethylbutane. Structures such as '2-ethylbutane' or '4-methylpentane' are repeats of these, drawn or numbered differently.

questions.stem: Which pair of compounds are structural isomers of each other?
questions.explanation: 2-methylpentane and 3-methylpentane are both C₆H₁₄ with different arrangements. Hexane is C₆H₁₄ but cyclohexane is C₆H₁₂, and butane has two more hydrogen atoms than but-1-ene.

questions.stem: What is the systematic name of CH₃CH₂CH(CH₃)CH₃?
questions.explanation: The longest chain has four carbon atoms, with a methyl group on carbon 2 when numbered from the nearer end. Numbering from the other end gives 3, which is not the lowest locant.

questions.stem: What is the systematic name of CH₂=CHCH₂CH₃?
questions.explanation: The chain has four carbons and the double bond starts at carbon 1 when numbered from the end nearer the double bond. 'But-3-ene' numbers from the wrong end.

questions.stem: What is the systematic name of CH₃CH=CHCH(CH₃)CH₃?
questions.explanation: The main chain has five carbons. The double bond gets the lowest number, so the chain is numbered from the left: the double bond starts at C2 and the methyl group is on C4. The double bond takes priority over the side chain in numbering.

questions.stem: A student names a compound 2-ethylbutane. What is its correct systematic name?
questions.explanation: Drawing 2-ethylbutane shows a longest chain of five carbons running through the ethyl group, with a methyl group on the middle carbon. A name must be based on the longest chain.

questions.stem: What is the systematic name of CH₃CH(C₂H₅)CH₂CH₂CH₃?
questions.explanation: The longest chain runs through the ethyl group and has six carbons, with a methyl group on carbon 3 from the nearer end. '2-ethylpentane' misses the longer chain, and '4-methylhexane' numbers from the wrong end.

questions.stem: What is the systematic name of CH₂=CH-CH=CH₂?
questions.explanation: Two double bonds make a diene, and an 'a' is added to the stem: buta-. The double bonds start at carbons 1 and 3. Numbering from the other end gives 2,4, which is higher, and a 1,4-diene of four carbons is impossible.

questions.stem: What is the condensed structural formula of 2,3-dimethylbut-2-ene?
questions.explanation: A four-carbon chain has its double bond between C2 and C3, and each of these carbons carries a methyl group. CH₂=C(CH₃)CH(CH₃)CH₃ is 2,3-dimethylbut-1-ene, and (CH₃)₂CHCH(CH₃)₂ has no double bond.

questions.stem: Why do the boiling points of the straight-chain alkanes increase as the chains get longer?
options: Longer chains have more C-H bonds, so more covalent bonds must break on boiling
Longer chains are more polar, so the dipole-dipole interactions are stronger
Larger molecules form more hydrogen bonds with neighbouring molecules
Larger molecules have more electrons, so the dispersion forces between them are stronger
questions.explanation: Alkanes are non-polar, so only dispersion forces act between their molecules, and these grow with the number of electrons and the contact area. Boiling separates molecules; it does not break covalent bonds.

questions.stem: The isomers pentane, 2-methylbutane and 2,2-dimethylpropane boil at 36, 28 and 10 °C. Which explanation fits this trend?
options: More branching makes the molecules more polar, so they repel and separate more easily
More branching weakens the C-C bonds, so less energy is needed to boil the compound
More branching makes the molecules more compact, so there is less contact and weaker dispersion forces
More branching adds more electrons to the molecules, so the dispersion forces become weaker
questions.explanation: The isomers have the same number of electrons, so the difference is shape. Compact, branched molecules touch over a smaller area than long chains, giving weaker dispersion forces and lower boiling points.

questions.stem: Hexane boils at 69 °C and octane at 126 °C. What is the best estimate of the boiling point of heptane?
questions.explanation: Heptane lies between hexane and octane in chain length, so its boiling point lies between theirs; it is in fact 98 °C. A value below 69 °C or above 126 °C would break the trend of the homologous series.

questions.stem: Petrol is mainly alkanes with 5 to 10 carbon atoms and is liquid at room temperature. Paraffin wax is mainly alkanes with 20 to 30 carbon atoms. Which is correct about the wax?
options: It is a solid, because its molecules are joined by covalent bonds between chains
It is a liquid, because all alkanes have the same strength of dispersion forces
It is a solid, because its larger molecules have stronger dispersion forces
It is a gas, because its larger molecules move faster and escape more easily
questions.explanation: Longer alkane molecules have more electrons and more contact, so the dispersion forces between them are strong enough to hold them in a solid at room temperature. There are no covalent bonds between separate wax molecules.

questions.stem: Which is the balanced equation for the complete combustion of octane?
questions.explanation: Complete combustion gives only CO₂ and H₂O. Sixteen C need 16 CO₂ and 36 H need 18 H₂O, which together contain 50 O atoms, so 25 O₂ are needed. Carbon monoxide forms only in incomplete combustion.

questions.stem: How many moles of oxygen are needed for the complete combustion of 1 mol of hexane, C₆H₁₄?
questions.explanation: C₆H₁₄ + 9.5O₂ → 6CO₂ + 7H₂O. The products contain 12 + 7 = 19 oxygen atoms, which is 9.5 O₂ molecules. Nineteen is the number of oxygen atoms, not molecules.

questions.stem: Octane burns completely: 2C₈H₁₈ + 25O₂ → 16CO₂ + 18H₂O. Use C = 12.01, H = 1.008, O = 16.00. What mass of carbon dioxide forms from 11.42 g of octane?
questions.explanation: M(C₈H₁₈) = 114.2 g mol⁻¹, so n = 11.42/114.2 = 0.1000 mol. Each mole gives 8 mol CO₂, so 0.800 mol × 44.01 = 35.2 g. Using a 1 : 1 ratio gives 4.40 g.

questions.stem: Besides being burnt as fuels, what is the other major use of hydrocarbons from petroleum?
options: As feedstock for making plastics and other chemicals
As fertilisers that supply nitrogen to crops
As the electrolyte in car batteries
As the raw material for making glass
questions.explanation: Hydrocarbons such as ethene and propene are the raw materials for polymers, solvents and many other chemicals. Burning them uses up a feedstock that cannot be replaced on human time scales.

questions.stem: What is the functional group of an alkene?
questions.explanation: A functional group is the part of a molecule that determines its characteristic reactions. In alkenes the C=C double bond undergoes addition reactions; alkanes, with only single bonds, do not.

questions.stem: But-2-ene reacts with hydrogen bromide in an addition reaction. What is the product?
questions.explanation: The H and Br add across the double bond between C2 and C3, so the Br ends up on carbon 2. 2,3-dibromobutane would form with Br₂, not HBr, and no double bond remains after addition.

questions.stem: Propene, CH₂=CHCH₃, reacts with bromine. What is the product?
questions.explanation: One bromine atom adds to each carbon of the double bond, which are carbons 1 and 2. 2-bromopropane would come from adding HBr, and 1,3-dibromopropane would need a bond to the end methyl group.

questions.stem: Which alkene gives 2-methylbutane when it reacts with hydrogen over a nickel catalyst?
questions.explanation: Adding H₂ keeps the carbon skeleton. 3-methylbut-1-ene, CH₂=CHCH(CH₃)CH₃, has the skeleton of 2-methylbutane. Pent-1-ene gives pentane, and the two methylpentenes give methylpentanes with six carbons.

questions.stem: What happens in addition polymerisation?
options: Long polymer chains are broken into smaller alkene monomers
Monomers with a C=C double bond join into a chain with no atoms lost
Monomers join into a chain and a small molecule such as water is released
Saturated monomers join into a chain by losing hydrogen atoms
questions.explanation: In addition polymerisation the double bond of each monomer opens and the monomers link, so the polymer contains every atom of the monomers. Losing a small molecule describes condensation polymerisation.

questions.stem: What is the monomer of poly(chloroethene), PVC?
questions.explanation: The name shows the monomer is chloroethene: ethene with one hydrogen replaced by chlorine. Chloroethane, CH₃CH₂Cl, has no double bond and cannot undergo addition polymerisation.

questions.stem: A section of polymer chain is -CH₂-CH(CH₃)-CH₂-CH(CH₃)-CH₂-CH(CH₃)-. What is its repeating unit?
questions.explanation: The two-carbon unit -CH₂-CH(CH₃)- repeats along the chain, showing the monomer is propene. -CH₂-CH₂-CH₂- has the right formula but the wrong structure, and the polymer has no double bonds.

questions.stem: A section of polymer chain is -CH₂-CH(CN)-CH₂-CH(CN)-CH₂-CH(CN)-. What is the monomer?
questions.explanation: Each repeating unit -CH₂-CH(CN)- comes from a monomer whose C=C double bond opened, so the monomer is CH₂=CHCN. CH₃CH₂CN is saturated and cannot add to a chain.

questions.stem: A poly(ethene) molecule forms from 5000 ethene molecules, C₂H₄ (M = 28.05 g mol⁻¹). What is its molar mass?
questions.explanation: Addition polymerisation loses no atoms, so the molar mass is 5000 × 28.05 = 1.40 × 10⁵ g mol⁻¹. Subtracting a water molecule for each link would apply only to a condensation polymer.

questions.stem: High-density polyethene (HDPE) is more rigid and melts at a higher temperature than low-density polyethene (LDPE). Why?
options: HDPE chains have many branches, which hold the chains apart and make them stiffer
HDPE chains are joined by many covalent cross-links that LDPE chains lack
HDPE chains contain polar groups, so they form hydrogen bonds between chains
HDPE chains have little branching, so they pack closely with stronger dispersion forces
questions.explanation: Unbranched HDPE chains line up closely, increasing the dispersion forces between them. The branches on LDPE keep chains apart. Both are made only of carbon and hydrogen, so neither forms hydrogen bonds.

questions.stem: Natural rubber becomes soft and sticky when warm. Vulcanisation heats it with sulfur. Why is vulcanised rubber harder and more elastic?
options: Sulfur breaks the long chains into shorter ones that pack more tightly together
Sulfur adds polar groups to the chains, which form hydrogen bonds with each other
Sulfur removes the double bonds, so the chains become straight and unbranched
Sulfur forms covalent cross-links between chains, so the chains cannot slide past each other
questions.explanation: Sulfur bridges covalently link neighbouring chains. The chains can stretch but spring back instead of sliding apart, and the rubber no longer softens when warm. Shorter chains would make it weaker, not harder.

questions.stem: What is a smart polymer?
options: A polymer whose properties change markedly in response to a stimulus such as heat or pH
A polymer made from renewable materials instead of fossil fuels
A polymer that breaks down completely in sunlight within a few days
A polymer whose chains are joined by many covalent cross-links
questions.explanation: Smart polymers respond to changes such as temperature, pH or light, for example by changing shape or swelling. Being made from renewable materials is a separate property.

questions.stem: Polyethene can be made from ethene produced from sugarcane ethanol instead of from petroleum. Which statement about this polyethene is correct?
options: It is chemically identical to polyethene from petroleum, so it is no more biodegradable
It is biodegradable, because it is made from a plant material
It has a different repeating unit, because its ethene came from a plant
It cannot be recycled with other polyethene, because its properties differ
questions.explanation: Ethene is the same molecule whatever its source, so the polymer is the same. Its advantage is a renewable feedstock, but it persists in the environment like any polyethene.

questions.stem: What is one disadvantage of producing polymers from renewable plant materials?
options: Plant materials contain no carbon, so carbon must be added separately
Growing the crops can compete with food production for farmland
The polymers always have weaker chains than those from petroleum
The process adds carbon to the atmosphere that was stored underground
questions.explanation: Crops grown as feedstock need land, water and fertiliser that could grow food. Releasing carbon stored underground is a disadvantage of fossil feedstocks, not renewable ones.

questions.stem: In molecules of HF, H₂O and NH₃, which atoms carry a partial positive charge (δ+)?
options: Neither, as the bonds are non-polar
The F, O and N atoms
questions.explanation: F, O and N are much more electronegative than H, so they pull the shared electrons towards themselves and become δ−, leaving each H atom δ+.

questions.stem: Which description of a hydrogen bond in liquid ammonia is correct?
options: A δ+ H atom on one molecule is attracted to the lone pair on N of a neighbouring molecule
A δ+ H atom on one molecule is attracted to a δ+ H atom on a neighbouring molecule
The N-H covalent bond within one molecule, which is strengthened by its polarity
Two N atoms on neighbouring molecules share a pair of electrons between them
questions.explanation: A hydrogen bond is a secondary interaction between molecules: a δ+ hydrogen bonded to N, O or F is attracted to a lone pair on a δ− N, O or F atom of another molecule. It is not the covalent bond within the molecule.

questions.stem: Ammonia, NH₃, boils at −33 °C, but methane, CH₄, of similar size, boils at −162 °C. Why?
options: Hydrogen bonds form between NH₃ molecules, but CH₄ has only dispersion forces
NH₃ has more electrons, so its dispersion forces are far stronger than CH₄'s
The N-H bonds are stronger than C-H bonds, so more energy is needed to boil it
CH₄ molecules are polar and repel each other, so they separate more easily
questions.explanation: With similar numbers of electrons, the dispersion forces are similar. NH₃ has N-H bonds and a lone pair, so its molecules hydrogen bond; CH₄ is non-polar. Boiling does not break covalent bonds.

questions.stem: Boiling points are H₂O 100 °C, HF 20 °C and NH₃ −33 °C. Which explanation fits this order best?
options: Each H₂O can form two hydrogen bonds on average, HF only one, and NH₃'s are weaker as N is less electronegative
HF forms the weakest hydrogen bonds, because fluorine is the least electronegative of the three atoms
H₂O has the most electrons of the three, so its dispersion forces are the strongest by far
NH₃ forms the most hydrogen bonds, as it has three H atoms, but they break apart most easily
questions.explanation: Water has two δ+ H atoms and two lone pairs, so it averages two hydrogen bonds per molecule. An HF hydrogen bond is individually strong, but each HF has only one H. N is less electronegative than O or F, and NH₃ has only one lone pair.
